thread.title: 3 Lessons Investment Pros Learned the Hard Way in 2018

title: 3 Lessons Investment Pros Learned the Hard Way in 2018

organizations.name: lessons investment pros learned the hard way

text:
3 Lessons Investment Pros Learned the Hard Way in 2018 By Jan. 8, 2019 5:00 a.m. ET Order Reprints Photograph by Hans Eiskonen Text size
Stocks dropped for the first time in a decade last year. Hedge funds, according to the Hedge Fund Research Global Index, dropped 6.7% in 2018 after falling 5.6% in the fourth quarter. In short, 2018 wasn’t a great year for Wall Street.
Barron’s asked several Wall Street analysts, investors, and market participants what they learned from the difficult environment. We received about a dozen responses, and few interesting themes emerged. When the stock market soars, sell some more
Many lamented the fact that they didn’t reduce exposure as the market rose, hitting all-time highs in September. Novalta Partners principal Barry Stewart summed it up with his 2019 resolution to maintain a larger cash balance and “wait for an obvious big, favorably skewed fundamental risk/reward opportunity, then invest.”
One possible reason for taking a “damn the torpedoes” approach to investing is FOMO (fear of missing out). We got the sense that there is a growing pressure on the pros to keep up with index funds and avoid underperforming investing benchmarks. After all, underperformance is an existential risk for money managers, but it isn’t for individual investors. That makes the advice “you can’t lose money taking a profit” worth remembering for everyone. Pay more attention to quality
“Balance sheets matter.” “Liquidity is an asset.” “Excessive leverage burned me.” These comments and others like them led us to believe investors will be looking for higher quality companies with less debt and strong free cash flow in 2019.
Barron’s noted several times last year that some “safe” stocks were anything but safe. Higher financial leverage magnified business problems and sent many debt laden companies like Anheuser-Busch InBev (BUD) or General Electric (GE) lower in 2018. Deceleration doesn’t mean recession
Another consensus opinion that emerged is that the economy isn’t all that bad. (Many investors also expressed the opinion that the Apple stock (AAPL) selloff is over done .)
When discussing the fear driving the fourth-quarter stock market selloff JO Hambro portfolio manager Arun Daniel expressed some dismay. “The companies we speak with are just not seeing significant declines in their backlogs,” he said. Daniel expects tax refunds and better-than-feared guidance from manufacturers to help consumer and industrial stocks early in 2019.
Others pointed out that a bear market doesn’t have to mean a recession is coming. Barron’s looked at 23 bear markets since 1929. We found that 15 were around or part of a recession. But that also means that more than one-third of the time, stock declines didn’t lead to a broader economic slowdown.
Finally, “it’s a funny market” was another common refrain. The speed with which the bear (or near-bear market depending, on your index of choice) developed left even market pros reeling. For instance, Apple had a trillion-dollar market cap on Oct. 3, and 50 days later it had lost one quarter of its value.
Of the 23 bear markets reference above, the average time for markets to drop 20% was about 175 days. But there is wide variation in that number. Several bear markets developed over 30 to 50 days—a few of those during the Great Depression. This time around, it took the Dow Jones Industrial Average 83 days to hit its low on Dec. 26.
So it seems that this market isn’t all that unusual. Even the pros can be prisoners of the moment.
I, for one, will resolve in 2019 to try my best to avoid becoming a prisoner of the moment. To paraphrase hockey great Wayne Gretzky, it’s better to keep one’s eyes on where the puck is headed and not where the puck has just been. After all, zigging when others zag, combined with a little price discipline, has been an excellent strategy for stock market success for many, many decades.
